transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-06
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Jared (RiverMark CTO), Priya (Lead ML), Liam (Infra), Sofia (PM)

Summary:
Quick weekly sync on POC latency tuning: review recent benchmark runs, discuss TTFT (time-to-first-token) and streaming tradeoffs, sequence length behavior, kernel choices and next steps for a kernel deep-dive and a third benchmark run. Some noisy transcription / crosstalk.

---- Transcript ----
[14:00] Maya: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, we got about 45 mins, quick recap of action items from last week then jump into the numbers. Connor is gonna walk through the kernel runs.
[14:01] Jared: Yep, sounds good. we've got Priya and Liam on the line, we'll try to be concise.
[14:02] Connor: cool, so just to remind — last run we did TTFT focused tests, streaming toggled on vs off, and sequence length sweeps 512/1024/2048. we also tried two kernel backends, the default fused-attn and the optimized matmul path. results are in the sheet.
[14:03] Priya: quick note, our infra noise yesterday might have inflated p95 by a bit — there was a host eviction during the 2k run so take that as a caveat.
[14:03] Connor: noted. ok slide into numbers, p50 for 512 was ~38ms with streaming disabled, TTFT around 110ms; with streaming on p50 dropped to 32ms but TTFT increased a bit because of the streaming handshake.
[14:05] Liam: when you say TTFT increased, like how much? our SLA is strict on human-perceived latency, first byte is important.
[14:05] Connor: yep, so TTFT moved to about 140ms in streaming mode for small payloads, because we buffer a small token batch before sending. for longer sequences streaming helps overall throughput but does add a small TTFT penalty.
[14:06] Maya: this is the classic tradeoff — streaming improves throughput and tail latencies for long sequences, but for low-latency first token you sometimes need tuned batch=1 paths or early flush.
[14:07] Priya: are there config knobs we can flip to reduce that handshake time? we care about p50 for first token under 120ms ideally.
[14:07] Connor: yes, we can reduce prefetch window and set early-flush threshold; also try the low-latency kernel variant we tested — it reduces TTFT by about 20ms on average but increases per-token compute slightly so cost goes up.
[14:08] Jared: cost vs latency — can you quantify? we have a cap on ops cost, we need numbers.
[14:08] Connor: roughly, low-latency kernel increased token compute ~6% in our test, so unit cost up ~5–7% but improves TTFT/p50 by 15–25ms depending on seq len. for 2k seq it actually helps tail a lot due to better memory layout.
[14:10] Sofia: is that impacted by quantization? we're running q4_0 emulation in our tests.
[14:10] Connor: good point — we ran both fp16 and q4 variants. q4 showed slightly higher variance on the matmul-optimized kernel, but fused-attn+q4 was stable. quantization changes kernel choice tradeoffs — some kernels don't support the quant path as efficiently.
[14:11] Priya: so for our current workload (avg seq 900, worst-case 2k) what's your recommendation?
[14:11] Connor: for avg 900 I'd suggest streaming on with early-flush at token window 8, use fused-attn kernel for q4 path. for the 2k tail runs, route those to a matmul-optimized variant or use dedicated capacity with the low-latency kernel enabled. you can do policy-based routing so long sessions go to dedicated pool.
[14:13] Jared: routing sounds good, can Redwood do auto-fallback if dedicated is saturated?
[14:13] Maya: yes, smart routing + automatic fallback to hosted compat models is supported, we can set fallbacks by latency tier or region.
[14:14] Liam: quick infra q — will switching kernels require model conversion or a new build?
[14:14] Connor: no conversion in most cases; kernel choice is runtime selected based on model arch and sequence length, but some optimized kernels require a model cast step for certain quant formats. we documented that in the bench notes.
[14:15] Priya: we saw a weird artifact in the transcript logs where KV cache was written heavy — transcript says K-V cash in the logs, just a small detection. but performance-wise we saw KV cache thrash at 2k sequences, which explains some p95 spikes.
[14:16] Connor: yeah KV cache pressure is real — we recommended chunked KV prefetching and aggressive cache eviction for very long sessions. that'll help p95.
[14:17] Jared: also security check — we need to confirm KMS integration and audit log retention before we ramp to dedicated. where are we on that?
[14:17] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer KMS and HSM integrations; we have SOC 2 docs and can share the compliance pack. audit logs retention configurable, we can match your 12 month retention requirement. we'll send the security pack today.
[14:18] Sofia: do you have any known competitor issues like PandaServe had with streaming TLS renegotiation? we want to avoid surprises.
[14:18] Connor: not on Redwood — we use connection pooling and TLS session reuse. we've seen PandaServe reports on renegotiation but that's not our architecture.
[14:19] Priya: ok back to tuning — one more ask: can you surface the kernel variant used per-run in the sheet? right now it's just numbers.
[14:19] Maya: yes we'll annotate the sheet with kernel name, quant setting, sequence distribution and whether streaming was on.
[14:20] Connor: and I'll add a column for TTFT components (handshake, model init, first decode) so you can see where time is spent.
[14:21] Liam: about the host eviction caveat — is there a suggested retry/backoff recommended for stable p95?
[14:21] Connor: yes, we recommend an exponential retry with jitter and prefer stateless requests for short sessions. for stateful long sessions, save checkpoints periodically.
[14:22] Jared: timeline — if we run the third benchmark next week and numbers look good, what's the gating to flip a canary to dedicated?
[14:22] Maya: typically we want 2 consistent runs with matched traffic and a security review complete. then we can provision a small dedicated pool (1–2 nodes) for canary, monitor for 48–72 hours and then scale.
[14:23] Priya: one silly nit — the demo harness has slightly different tokenization settings than our prod pipeline; could that explain some discrepancy in token counts?
[14:24] Connor: absolutely, tokenization differences can change sequence length distribution; we'll align tokenization and push a script to normalize counters.
[14:24] Maya: ok let's recap next steps — Maya will share kernel tuning notes and the annotated benchmark sheet; Priya will run the 3rd run with 2k sequence and streaming enabled; Connor to prepare kernel deep-dive and list of variants; Liam to confirm VPC peering scheduling.
[14:25] Jared: sounds good. any final blockers?
[14:25] Priya: just the infra noise — I'll try to isolate host issues before next run.
[14:26] Maya: great. Connor, can you schedule the kernel deep-dive for the week of Apr 12?
[14:26] Connor: yes I'll send a calendar invite, expect 60–90 mins with some perf traces.
[14:27] Sofia: thanks everyone.
[14:27] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the sheet and security docs.
[14:28] Jared: thanks, bye.

End of call.
